Well, for one thing, heart attacks don't work like that. A car horn isn't going to suddenly block someone's arteries.

Secondly, and a brief explanation about how our law works, it comes down to a question of forseeability. Let's try a different scenario. The car alarm beeps and lights flash. It scares a bunch of birds, that disturb a bee-hive, that stings a dog, which bites the victim who dies three months later of rabies. Is the owner of the car liable? Is proximate causation established that having a car alarm would trigger a chain of events that would cause a person to die? No. Why? Because it wasn't reasonably foreseeable. We are exposed to sudden noises and frightening elements all of the time. It is part of life and the world around us. The owner of the car could not have possibly anticipated that a beeping horn could have caused such a chain of events to occur that would have caused this person's death.

Now, let's say someone put a joy buzzer device inside of a lion's den at a zoo with the goal of making a loud frightening sound to rattle the jimmies of the lion tamer when they entered the den, and that sound also scared the lion who then proceeded to maul the tamer. Reasonable foreseeable? Possibly.

But back to what we are talking about. Bike owner shocks the thief while he is riding the bike, thief falls off, hits his head on a rock and dies. Estate sues. Is delivering the electric shock a proximate causation to the cause of death (hitting his head after falling off the bike caused by the shock)? Absolutely. Why? Because it is entirely reasonable that it could be foreseen that if you deliver an electric shock to somebody who is riding a bicycle that they might fall off of that bike, and in doing so they could hit their head on a rock, or the pavement, or a tree in front of them causing them injury. It doesn't matter what that injury is (from a scrape or broken bones to crushed skull), it just has to be reasonably foreseeable to establish causation.
